claims_disputed.claim: Scoring the retrieved set instead of the answer's citations inverts the architecture ranking (GraphRAG context precision 0.12-0.23 vs citation precision 0.48-0.65)
claims_disputed.reason: Table 2 tabulates context precision for GraphRAG only. The statement that 'by context precision GraphRAG is the worst pipeline in every setting' (§5.2), and hence the inversion of the full five-pipeline ranking, is asserted in text, not shown. The effect is also partly built in: GraphRAG passes up to 15 context IDs against vanilla's top-5 (§3.1), so its context precision must be lower whenever gold sets are small. The GraphRAG-internal gap (3-5x precision enrichment from context to citations) is solid. The ranking inversion is only moderately supported.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: No pipeline checks the IDs it cites against the link store before answering. Citations are checked against gold only by the evaluator (§3.3), so 'verified links' is never tested. The graph-walk vs dense comparison the review cites is already credited under P07, and the links are requirement-to-requirement/verification, not to code. The paper uses traceability as its task without an isolating comparison of the pattern.

missed_issues: The learned router does not beat the best single pipeline. Adaptive-V2 overall citation F1 is 0.559/0.569 (Table 4) against fixed GraphRAG at 0.551/0.571 (Table 2). The headline '59%/55% gap closure' is measured from the weak rule-based router V1, and the routing target is derived from the full matrix rather than per fold. Routing (P23, not tagged) adds nothing here.

The 'adaptive' row in Table 1 (per-stratum mean about 0.44 local, 0.47 Azure) matches the rule-based V1 overall F1 (0.439/0.468). It is worse than both vanilla and GraphRAG on 1-2-hop strata, so in the main table routing is net harmful.

There is no deterministic traversal baseline. The corpus is authored as a typed link graph stored in Neo4j, so a Cypher query from the anchor requirement answers trace chains exactly. The paper never tests whether LLM retrieval is needed to recover chains that already exist as explicit links.

The agentic LangGraph loop costs 0.19-0.30 citation F1 against one-shot dense retrieval on 1-2-hop queries under both embedders (Table 1), with no mechanism and no token or latency cost reported for any pipeline.

Queries, gold chains and corpus are all generated by GPT-5.4, which also answers and judges. The hop-decodability result (C4) and the per-stratum difficulty may be artifacts of how the generator phrases multi-hop questions, as the authors concede for C4 only.
note: I agree with the verdict, no-COI call, the contradicts stance on P18, mixed on P07 and P06, weak for the faithfulness-trend and router claims, and moderate for the judge-drift and winner claims. The frozen-input 11-week re-judge (kappa 0.14 and about 0 against a 0.76 same-day floor) is the cleanest result. I lower the 'ranking inversion' claim to moderate because only GraphRAG's context precision is tabulated and the inversion is partly a consequence of its larger context cap. P42 should be introduces, since no arm verifies cited links. The review missed that the learned router merely ties the best fixed pipeline and that the main-table router is worse than vanilla on short hops. My relevance is 2, not 3: the corpus is a synthetic aerospace requirement graph with no code, and what transfers to the team is evaluation practice rather than a traceability design.
